The Astral Express had long since departed, the Trailblazers only occasionally popping in to say hello, busy travelling the vast cosmos, and in its awake the true nature of Amphoreus was revealed, and after all the heirs had died to pave the way for Phainon to bring Era Nova to completion, only to be brought back to life abruptly to fight an awakened Lord Ravager, Irontomb, along side the Trailblazers and several others from beyond the beautiful, and apparently, the fake skies of Amphoreus. 

At the moment, it was all too much to process, everything happening all at once, too many important figures revealing themselves, Phainon's long supposedly dead sister, Cyrene, appearing, and Phainon himself fighting from within the monstrous body of Irontomb. But it all ended well, excluding the various injuries they all gained during the long and excruciating battle, and Mydei had reunited with Phainon, and the other Heirs in tears, and for the Genius Society member, the purple witch, to turn all of them and Amphoreus from strings of codes, to living, breathing and bleeding humans.

So yes, Amphoreus’ current peace was well sought after, and after three years of sleepless nights, Aglaea, after discussing with the Trailblazers, had opened up Amphoreus for visitors beyond the sky. Many showed up, curious about the stimulated world that had attracted the attention of not just one, or two, but four different Aeons.

Mydei who had long since accepted he wouldn't stay alive to see Phainon bring about Era Nova, so it took a while to adjust to the idea that the black tide wasn't no longer a problem, the Flame Chase was completed, and he and the other heirs were finally free of the duty that had burdened them ever since they were selected for the experiment.

So what did Mydei do? 

Well, he got married three years ago, as soon as he had understood everything that had happened, and things had settled down enough to call it peace, and he talked everything out. 

The talking was the hard part, Mydei, too used to hiding his emotions behind his facade, edges all rough by years of loss and suffering. His conversation partner wasn't any better, breaking down in tears in Mydei's arms.

Who did he marry?

Phainon ofcourse. It was no exaggeration to say that he had fallen in love with the alpha after they fought for ten days and ten nights straight, with no clear victor in sight.

Alphas were arrogant, with no skill to back up that confidence and arrogance, and Mydei, as angry as he was at the time, could admit he was impressed. Phainon was also impressed, and eager, and none of that changed even as he learned Mydei was an Omega. 

It was inevitable, in all honesty. 

After always making time for each other, despite how bloodied and bruised they were from missions, Mydei allowing himself to be dragged along by Phainon for anything, their arguments and sparrs going out of control, and getting scolded by Aglaea for public damage, when he felt his vivid blue eyes fall upon Mydei in crowds, always seeking him out, as he vigorously defended Mydei and the other Kremnoans, going out of his way to call Mydei beautiful as the two of them play the city's children drag them into their games.

In every sparr, cocky smirks, and moments between the two of them. Mydei had never said it, never dared, forcing the words down his throat whenever they came up. 

Because even though both of knew just how much they cared about each other, how both of their feelings were reciprocated but never once did they cross the line of friendship to lovers, because of the prophecy, and this invisible noose of fate above them that they feared will suffocate if they ever dare to be selfish for once in their life.

So the two of them did work hard to get where they are right now: married for three years, happy, warm and secure in their devotion and love for each other, and their first child growing in Mydei's belly, warm, protected and healthy.

If it was one thing to know you were the omega of Phainon's affections, but another thing to allow him to smother you with his love, his Phainon who never did learn how to hold his grief and rage without welding it like a sword, his Phainon who would rather die than never allow himself to be selfish.

Hmm, okay. Mydei couldn't criticise him for his selflessness, because he too was like that to a certain extent.

But the extent to which he was protective was surprising, because Phainon very rarely got angry, always with a charming smile present on his face. He wasn't a pacifist by any means, but very rarely did he get angry to the point of raising his voice or lashing out physically. Besides, the alpha didn't even need to raise his voice for people to be scared, the even and steady tone paired with his vivid and cold blue eyes more often than not, did the trick.

Sometime around his fifteenth week of pregnancy, around the time his food cravings had stopped and been replaced by a craving for his husband instead, he did wonder what would finally cause his devoted and pleasant husband to finally snap, and Mydei had gotten the answer for that twelve weeks later. 

————

The sunlight from the Dawn Device was warm on the streets of Okhema, spilling over the sights of Marmoreal Market alive as always, across the colors of the market stalls – silks in every tone one could ask for, baskets piled high with pomegranates, figs, goat cheese, and fresh daily produce. Over the calls of the vendors and the words of the residents going about their day, the clang of hammering bronze could be heard, acting as nothing more than background noise. 

It was all familiar, the peace they had all sought after.

Mydei had thought it would feel strange, walking these streets with the burden of duty heavy on his shoulders, but it was even stranger as he walked with his twenty-seven-week pregnant belly. But Cyrene’s arm was lopped around his own, stuck to his side as she kept up a constant stream of words, from commentary on the products on sale, to some snippets of conversation she overheard, or even childhood memories of the siblings in Aedes Elysiae. It was all too familiar to the routine he shared with Phainon even before the reveal, and Cyrene’s blue eyes were wide and happy as she stared up at him whenever he replied with his thoughts, a replica of Phainon's eyes that he had fallen in love, and it was another reminder that they shared blood despite their physical differences. 

Next to them, Castorice had a basket tucked under her arm as she glanced around the market looking for the ingredients they wanted. Cipher should also be here with them, but Aglaea had requested her help with an errand, with the promise of jewels as compensation. Phainon would have been right next to Mydei, strong arm wrapped around his waist as they walked, but he too was also tasked with a quick errand, and he had reluctantly left, promising to be back soon with a soft kiss at Mydei's temple, which lingered long enough for Cyrene to giggle.

The voices of merchants calling out prices, Cyrene’s soft voice right next to him, and the scent of fresh bread on the breeze, finally made him almost feel like he belonged to this place, instead of the sense of loneliness that comes with making foreign lands your home, all for the sake of your people.

Even now, as he walked, he could see his people mingling with the crowds. A young child ran past them, giggling as he tugged his mother along with him, a Kremnoan woman called Arete, who offered her crown prince a guilty smile as she let herself be tugged along by the child.

“You’re smiling,” Cyrene observed brightly, as she reached up to tuck a long strand of blond hair behind his ear, "That's good. I was scared it would be too overstimulating for you.”

Mydei shook his head with a soft smile. “I’m okay, I really am,” he assured, “I can still walk, and I'm used to all the different scents in Marmoreal market, so it's not too overbearing.”

“That’s good, I would hate to be the reason why my brother-in-law feels suffocated under all these scents just because I asked you to make some desserts.” She shook her head as she stared out into the crowd, “They don't try to control their scents, do they?” she remarked with a small laugh.

The steady footsteps of Castorice made both of them look up. “Lord Mydei, Lady Cyrene,” she greeted, and held out the basket for both of them to see what she had brought. “I brought some pistachios for Lady Trianne as well as some apples.”

“They look really good, Castorice,” Cyrene praised, one hand reaching in to pull out an apple. “Keep this up and I'm going to start bothering you for my shopping quests and my sweet tooth.” 

The alpha in question blushed at the genuine praise, as she nervously tugged at her long lilac strands. “It's not a bother, Lady Cyrene. I do enjoy baking, and you have Lord Mydei to thank for that since he's the one who taught me.”

“It's nothing, Castorice, stop praising me like I gave you something extraordinary, when it's just a few hours of my day spent with my friend,” he chided.

The woman only smiled apologetically as Cyrene slipped the apple back into the basket and pulled out a slip of paper.

“What else do we need?” the pink-haired woman asked curiously. Mydei glanced down at the basket, “We already got everything for the koptoplakous, now we just need–”

“Oranges, cloves and rose water for the vasilopita,” Castorice finished. She shifted the basket under her arm, “Rose water shouldn't be hard to find at all. I believe it's somewhere about here,” and she stepped forward, leading Mydei and Cyrene along with her.

Few people stopped to offer wishes and congratulations, or even just to say hello as they walked by.

Mydei shifted ever so slightly, his free hand curling around his swollen belly to support it. Cyrene scanned the bustling streets as Castorice engaged in a conversation with an older vendor.

“You know,” Cyrene started with a little grin, her blue eyes sparkling, “I keep forgetting just how famous you and Phainon are, maybe because I've just gotten so used to you two bickering and playing around with each other. The people of Okhema do love you and–”, her eyes drifted towards his belly, “–your unborn baby,” she finished, a wide smile on her face. “The baby is going to grow up so loved, ah, just thinking about it makes me feel emotional,” she sniffed once, as if to prove her point. 

“I can see just how much you and Phainon love each other, and just how much love you have for your baby, even though they haven't even been born yet. Both of you are going to be such good parents and I can't wait to be an amazing aunt! Such a shame you can't eat that many sweets though, but! I'm always here for that,” she chirped. 

Mydei snorted, as he raised an eyebrow, amused, “Is this your way of saying you want to have more than one niece or nephew?”

The omega stared at her nails, suddenly finding them very interesting as she shyly looked up to meet golden eyes, “Well, I won't deny that it sounds nice, but I would also get more sweets along with it, so maybe, yes,” she admitted with a laugh.

His cheeks warned, “I don't have to be pregnant for you to overindulge on sweets, I'm more than willing to make them for you.”

“Aww, thank you, but even if you don't say anything, I sometimes feel bad because you and Phainon take such good care of your bodies, and then here I am,” she sighed, flipping a stubborn lock of hair over her shoulder.

“I don't,” Mydei argued. “Well, I used to, but besides too many sweets, isn't that terrible.”

“Yes, it is!” Cyrene replied dramatically, pressing a hand to her chest. “Do you know how embarrassing it would be to explain to Okhema how one of its heroes overindulged on sweets to the point where she's more candy than human? I’d never live it down.” She sniffed haughtily.

“Hmm, your hair does match the colour of the frosting brought back to us by Stelle, so in my opinion, you already are a dessert.” That earned him a very, very light smack on his arm and a large pout with mock tears. He laughed, his cheeks warm with amusement. “You’re ridiculous.”

“I prefer whimsical,” Cyrene corrected, her grin widening at his laugh, but then she lowered her voice just a touch, leaning closer. “But, Mydei, I like seeing you smile like this. You’re always so busy helping around. Sometimes it’s nice just to be a family, hm?”

Before Mydei could reply, two little children ran up, both familiar faces, Orion and Adonis. He had played house with them often, dragged into it by the entire group of children and their unfathomable stubbornness and insistence.

“Lord Mydei! Oh, hi Lady Cyrene!” Orion greeted, tugging eagerly at his hand, brown eyes wide with joy “It's been so long since we last saw you! Maia misses you! and–” the boy was shoved aside by an overly enthusiastic Adonis, who grasped the fabric of his chiton, “When the baby is born, can we play house again? This time we can all be big siblings, not just Lydia!”

The earnestness in their voices tugged at his heart. Mydei bent ever so slightly, mindful of his belly, and smoothed a hand over Orion’s curly hair, who then proceeded to stick his tongue out smugly at Adonis. “I missed you all as well,” he admitted, “I think it would be lovely, but only if you all promise not to boss the baby around too much.”

“We will!

“We promise Lord Mydei and–”

“Adonis!” a sharp voice yelled out, causing both adults to look up curiously and both boys to flinch as they turned around.

“Oh shoot! That's my mom, sorry we gotta go, bye Lord Mydei, Lady Cyrene!” Adonis apologized profusely before grabbing Orion's hand and tugging him along. Orion allowed himself to be dragged along, turning his head to wave back at them.

“Bye!”

“Bye!” Cyrene echoed, smiling widely before she sighed, her hand slipping lightly into the crook of Mydei’s arm once again. “Do you see it? Despite so many rumours and prejudice against you and your people, you’ve already woven yourself so tightly into this city. Even the little ones are planning their games around you.”

Mydei tilted his head, smiling faintly. “I have always loved children, they don't know how to hate, only how to love. That’s not a bad thing, is it?”

“No, of course,” Cyrene said softly, squeezing his arm. “It’s beautiful. I'm sorry, it's just one thing to see it through someone else's memory, but something completely different when experiencing it for yourself. I just—” She broke off, her eyes misty with a fondness that made Mydei’s chest ache. “I believe my brother's behaviour has started to influence me as well, I'm afraid. I love you too much not to worry a little, that’s all.”

A vendor they were passing by interrupted with a cheery call, pressing a handful of figs into Mydei’s hands, which he gracefully denied, and the vendor didn't even blink, passing them onto Cyrene with a wide smile, who accepted one fight and graciously turned down the rest.

She popped it into her mouth and hummed in delight. 

Up ahead, Castorice was eagerly listening to a woman talk about different fabrics and craft materials.

Cyrene swallowed and laughed, light and bright as a bell, as she followed his gaze. “It's so rare to see Castorice so animated,” she commented brightly, “But shame, you did miss out on a really good fig Mydei,” she tutted. 

“Do you think the baby will ever forgive me if I eat more than one of the figs meant for them before we get home?”

“You wouldn’t dare,” Mydei teased.

“Wouldn’t I?” Cyrene winked, already pretending to sneak one out of a nearby stand, before relenting and tucking her hand behind her back. “Fine, fine. I’ll wait. But only because I like being your favorite sister-in-law, and the baby's favorite aunt.”

“You’re my only sister-in-law,” Mydei pointed out, amused.

“Exactly. See how easy I’ve made things for you?” she winked at him brightly.

Mydei shook his head fondly, warmth curling in his chest. Cyrene had always had that effect on everybody really, turning worry into laughter, turning the heaviness of duty into something lighter, bearable.

It was then, as the moment of laughter faded into the hum of the market, that an old woman’s voice carried to them. She stood by a stall of dried herbs, her shawl a faded shade of indigo, her eyes sharp despite her years.

“Be careful, heroes,” she said, her words clear and deliberate, despite the worry in her sharp, cloudy eyes. “Not all who smile at you mean you well.”

The cheer of the market dimmed around her voice. 

Mydei tilted his head in question at her words, free arm subconsciously curling around his belly. Cyrene blinked, her hand tightening ever so slightly on Mydei’s arm.

“What's wrong?” Castorice asked as she joined them, a basket heavy with her purchases. She shifted her attention to the old lady in question, as Mydei shook his head ever so slightly as an answer to her question.

“Careful?” Cyrene asked gently, tilting her head. “Why would you say that?”

But before the old woman could answer, raised voices cut across the street – a man’s arrogant tone came, a voice so loud and grating it seemed designed to draw every gaze. It dripped with disdain as he argued with a vendor over her wares.

“This–” a man’s accent thickened the word like honey, though his voice was anything but pleasant to hear, too whiny and high-pitched, “–is supposed to be food? By the Amber Lord, what filth is this? You call this weaving? This is a child’s work! Where I come from, even the beggars would spit on such trash!”

The three demigods froze at the same time, and simultaneously, their heads turned.

Just a few stalls down, an average-looking man, with an average build, dressed in clothes that were very expensive from first glance, loomed over a vendor’s stand, his voice rising in arrogant disdain. His suit bore the crest he had learned to recognize: the insignia of the Interastral Peace Corporation – the IPC. The Trailblazers had already warned the demigods about them, and their greed and exploitative measures for expansion and resources. They had begun to creep into Amphoreus now that its borders were open. Around him hovered several armored guards, their uniforms strange to local eyes.

The vendor he berated was a young woman, perhaps no older than the youngest soldier in the Kremnoan detachment, who clutched her goods to her chest as if that would shield them from his scorn. The crowd around them had gone silent, onlookers shrinking back with disapproval and unease, some anger present among them.

The man, whose scent was all over the place, spread his arms in mock incredulity. “And you dare sell this? Do you even know what quality is? Where I am from, the IPC supplies true goods. Better fabric, better food, better trade – not this provincial, homemade scrap.”

When the vendor tried to murmur out a shaky defense, his hand shot out, seizing her wrist. She cried out, dropping half the bundles she held.

Mydei did not think twice as he reached them in three swift steps, Cyrene and Castorice moving in perfect sync with him. The crowd parted without hesitation, making way for the demigods. They knew them, and more importantly, they trusted them.

“Release her,” Mydei warned. He didn't raise his voice, but the entire market seemed to draw its breath when he spoke.

The man, a beta turned, was still gripping the girl’s wrist. His sneer was wide and contemptuous, his teeth glinting in the sun. “Ah, and who is this? A hero that came to scold me?” and then he seemed to have noticed the women right beside him, “No wait, a group of heroes coming to scold me, huh?” he laughed obnoxiously, the sound rippling through the crowd. Mydei saw more anger now, but he didn't bite the bait, only glaring coolly at the man.

Castorice’s gentle smile was gone, replaced by a cold glare that could have cut through steel itself as she remained by his side. Cyrene extracted her arm from Mydei's and drifted ever so closer to the young woman as she whimpered, trying to twist free.

For a moment, the man seemed oblivious, but then one of his guards leaned close, whispering into his ear. Another did the same, their faces pale as they spoke, and Mydei's keen ears caught the name – Skott. The pair of glasses covered his eyes, but Mydei could feel them flickering from the vendor to Mydei, studying his face, the two women, then lingered with arrogant interest on the curve of his belly.

“Oh wait,” he gasped, voice dripping with mockery. “So these are the famed demigods of Amphoreus, and I have the honor of meeting them in such a charming and hideous place. How… quaint.”

Out of the corner of his eyes, Mydei saw one too many people bristling in anger as the word ugly left his mouth.

Obvious to it all, he shoved the vendor away with careless force. She stumbled, but Cyrene was already there, catching her with gentle arms. Tears trembled on her lashes as Cyrene wrapped her arms around the woman, gently whispering soft words of comfort in her ear as she tugged her away from the IPC. A teenage boy quietly stepped up to pick up the bundles dropped by her, his eyes sharp as he glared at the foreigners.

Skott spread his arms, as if magnanimous. “There, released. I imagine you’ll run to that demigod now, and file your complaint, and whine about how a guest mistreated your people?” He sneered. “Will your little demigod file a complaint against me to my superiors? Go on them. My superiors don't give a damn about common folks like her. Tell my superiors. See if I care.”

Mydei met his gaze, unimpressed and slightly amused. How ironic of him to call Aglaea little when he was barely taller than Castorice, and Cyrene, who seemed to have made the same conclusion, snickered under her breath as she joined him again. Her face was a mask of serenity.

His silence must have unsettled him. The crowd held its breath, and Skott, who seemed unused to being met with composure instead of deference, felt the need to push harder.

The market square had a rhythm of its own, a tide of voices, laughter, and haggling that usually drowned out everything else, but now, the stillness had spread. Even people near the edge of the market, far away from the confrontation, paused mid-bargain, mid-step, mid-sentence. The silence pulled in strangers, other foreigners, soldiers, neighbors, children, even vendors who craned their heads up to watch.

Mydei did not move, did not flinch, unimpressed even as Skott smirked at him with the kind of arrogance that came from too much unearned power.

“Funny,” Skott drawled, his words sharpened by the hush of the onlookers. “I expected more from Amphoreus’s so-called heroes. All that praise, all those songs, all this praise for you left and right – yet here you are, tongue-tied in a marketplace. Do you need one of your men to answer for you? Or has pregnancy finally taken the sharpness from your mind?”

A gasp rolled through the crowd. Some parents drew their children closer, muttering curses under their breath, as guards shifted uneasily, fists clenching. Mydei even saw his people bristling at the words, stepping forward, but they stepped back as Mydei glanced at them quickly.

Mydei shifted his eyes back to the man and smiled, and in his head, he quickly compared the blabbering man in front of him to his husband, and well, he had to bite the inside of his cheek to stop himself from laughing out loud.

“I am more than capable of talking for myself. If anything, you should consider paying one of your guards to talk for you since they clearly pay attention and caution, unlike you. For someone from the IPC, your work style doesn't match up. You didn't even know who we were until your men told you. Pathetic for a man who wishes to build economic relations in Amphoreus, really.”

Cyrene laughed aloud at his words as Skott flushed bright red, sputtering in outrage. Castorice quickly covered up her chuckle with her hand, as the crowd, quiet at first, then louder, started whispering and laughing amongst each other. A few clapped their hands over their mouths, but others laughed openly and mockingly.

Skott’s smirk faltered, his jaw twitching. He opened his mouth, but Cyrene snapped her fingers as though suddenly struck by a realisation, tilted her head slightly and spoke first, her soft voice pitched loud enough to carry across the crowd.

“Wait! I know you!” Cyrend exclaimed loudly and conversationally, as though they were all old friends. “It took me a moment, sorry, but now it’s all clear. Silly me for forgetting such a story! Stelle told me all about you once! About a certain IPC member who placed a bet with her when she was in Aurum Alley, on the Xianzhou Luofu, someone who bit off more than he could chew and severely underestimated her and lost.” She turned towards the crowd, smiling widely, “Does anybody want to hear it?”

 "Of course we do, Lady Cyrene!” a man called out, and the crowd leaned in instinctively. Even Mydei arched a brow, a flicker of amusement crossing his beautiful features.

Skott yelped, bright red “Y-you! You–” he sputtered, as he pointed a hand at Cyrene, who ignored it with ease, delighted as the man choked on his own words.

Cyrene grinned, darker than her usual pleasant and bright smile. “It’s simple really, Skott over here placed a bet with the Stelle and her friends stating if the merchant guild of Aurum Alley failed to pay back all the money owed to the IPC, they would have to apologize to all the residents of Aurum Alley and bark and howl like a dog while on their knees, with Skott himself stating he would do so if he lost the bet. The punishment was so simple! In front of a whole crowd, a very angry crowd by the way, apparently, he purposefully sabotaged Stelle; he had to get down on all fours and bark like a dog. Not once. Not twice. No, no, he had to do it until the angry crowd was satisfied. He made a very convincing dog.”

For a heartbeat, the silence held, suspended on the edge of expectation, then it shattered. 

The crowd erupted into laughter all at once, a wave that rolled through the hall with startling force. It rose like a single voice, booming off the walls. Shopkeepers leaned against their stalls, shoulders shaking, as children clutched at each other in delight, some people doubled over while others wiped their eyes, and for a moment, the sound was so overwhelming it felt almost alive.

“Why don't you bark for us now, Skott?” one man yelled out, “We need entertainment.”

“Yeah! Go for it, little boy! I'll even tie a collar around your neck if it's really good.”

Mydei bit the inside of his cheek to stop himself from laughing too hard. Castorice’s shoulders were shaking with the force of her silent laughter, as Skott went red, his face burning hotter than Chartonus’ forge, as he glared at the crowd, at Mydei and a smug Cyrene. His guards stared fixedly at the cobblestones.

“Lies!” he snapped, his voice cracking under the weight of humiliation. “Baseless slander—”

“Childish slander,” Mydei interrupted smoothly, tilting his head. His golden eyes glittered with mirth. “Perhaps. But then again, it does suit you, doesn’t it? I have experience dealing with men like you. Tell me, Skott, did you wag your tail too?”

The square erupted again as the laughter rolled louder and sharper. Some youths wolf-whistled, as one woman shouted out mockingly, “Be a good dog now!”.

Skott’s composure shattered like glass. He trembled with fury, his fists clenching and unclenching, his jaw working without words. He stepped forward, but Mydei didn't move an inch and stood calm, serene, his cruel smile cutting deeper with every heartbeat. He had faced death and horrors beyond comprehension for this pathetic little man, an insignificant beta, to scar him.

And in that silence that followed the laughter, his voice turned ugly.

“You mock me because you’re afraid,” he hissed, though the tremor in his voice betrayed him. “You stand here pretending strength, but I see through it. An omega like you, fighting when you should be nesting, flaunting yourself in the streets when you should be hidden, shameless behaviour like that, hah! You’ll end up leaving that child motherless, neglected and lonely.

The crowd’s mirth soured at once. The hush that followed was thick with anger. Mothers scowled openly as the people muttered darkly under their breath, and even children stilled in their parents’ arms.

“You–” Arete started, her face tight with anger, but she was silenced by the people beside her.

Cyrene shifted next to him, beautiful face pale with anger, as her fingers flexed. The smell of rot and decay intensified from Castorice as she frowned, fingers clenching tightly.

For having the anger and attention of such a large crowd Skott didn't flatter.

But Mydei only smiled wider, unimpressed with his attempt at dismantling him with words. Hah! The man would have to live for another hundred years before his words could even hope to match the scorn he had faced from the Council of Elders and the nobles of Okhema.

“Neglected, you say?” he asked, voice soft and biting. “I suppose it takes neglect to recognize neglect. Tell me, Skott, how many times did your mother drop you on your head for you to grow so arrogant? Oh, wait, did your mom even hold you at all?”

Never mind the fact that he had only his mother's warmth for a fleeting moment.
